column3: The condemned are cast into the same blazing place, whose roar and boiling establish the immediate fire setting.
Casting the ear toward a reminder does not clarify forced casting into punishment or the cry for destruction.
Its constricted state supplies a real resonance with narrowness, though it describes the Prophet's distress rather than punitive enclosure.
The direct continuation answers the cry here: they must not call for one destruction, but for many.
The preceding denial of the Hour and preparation of a blaze supply the judgment frame for being thrown into it.
The title of Dhu al-Qarnayn has no material link to confinement, binding, or the punishment cry.
It repeats the call for destruction as the response of one facing the fire.
Courtly demands for ornaments and accompanying angels do not clarify the condemned being bound together.
It depicts criminals bound together in fetters on the judgment day, directly paralleling the focus's chained state.
Binding in fetters is shared imagery, but the verse concerns restrained devils rather than human punishment in Hell.
The immediately preceding verse presents the distant fire's rage and exhalation, completing the scene into which they are thrown.
The fire itself calls those who turned away, matching the focus's reversal in which the condemned call for destruction.
Defeat at a specified place does not develop the focus's fire, enclosure, or invocation.
Within the same denunciation sequence, the mockers are told they will know when they see the punishment.
A summons to faith under a covenant is not materially related to punitive calling or confinement.
Mary's withdrawal to a remote place is unrelated to the condemned's narrow enclosure.
The magicians' choice over who casts first has no judgment or confinement connection.
The caller summons people to a dreadful event, a related judgment-day summons without the focus's binding and enclosure.
A defeated faction at that place offers no substantive parallel to the focus scene.
The mockery of the Messenger belongs to the local rejection context but adds no direct element of the punishment scene.
The wide earth becoming constricted and the people's retreat provide a strong spatial reversal, though in a battlefield rather than Hell.
Elevation to a high place is the opposite movement from being thrown into a narrow place.
The Messenger's warning role is part of the surrounding surah context but does not specify the focus's consequence.
Moses calls Pharaoh doomed, connecting obstinate rejection with destruction without the focus's enclosed-fire image.
The destruction of a corrupt town shares the consequence of judgment but not the focus's particular scene.
Destroyed generations offer a general warning of ruin, not a parallel to binding or calling for destruction.
The annihilation of earlier generations is a broad judgment parallel only.
Mary's separation to an eastern place does not illuminate punitive spatial confinement.
The wrongdoer's regret on the Day of Judgment develops the same surah's aftermath of rejection, though not its fire imagery.
The destruction of past generations is too general to clarify the focus's specific punishment action.
The false attribution of a child to the Merciful does not address the focus's judgment mechanics.
The magicians being cast into prostration is voluntary worship, not forcible casting into punishment.
Those who invoked false partners find them absent, a related collapse of invocation in the judgment context.
Human inability to control transport is unrelated to being chained together in Hell.
The objection to the Messenger's ordinary life belongs to the local disbelief sequence but does not explain the focus scene.
Destroyed generations called out when there was no longer a time of escape, closely matching a futile last cry.
Severe testing and shaking of believers do not develop the focus's punishment or confinement.
Satanic suggestion being cast into a prophet's wish has no relevant relation to the condemned being cast into fire.
Those called besides God possess nothing, reinforcing the failure of appeals directed away from the true judge.
Those gathered face-down toward Hell are assigned the worst place and path, directly extending the focus's forced movement into Hell.
It is part of the nearby dispute over worldly signs but does not add to the confinement or destruction cry.
Earlier destroyed generations do not return to later people, a substantial but general judgment consequence.
The casting of magical objects is unrelated to the focus's punitive casting and binding.
The described devils as builders and divers do not clarify the focus's prison-like condition.
Noah's public call is a prophetic invitation, not a failed cry from punishment.
Moses' command to cast is part of the magic contest and has no judgment connection.
The universal warning function supplies the proclamation whose rejected audience reaches the punishment described in the focus.
The constriction of the chest supplies a distinct but meaningful resonance with the focus's narrowness.
Broad paths through the earth contrast with, rather than clarify, the narrow punitive enclosure.
Secure travel through visible towns does not bear on the focus's binding or fire.
The challenge whether idols hear an invocation exposes the incapacity of false addressees, relevant to futile calling.
God's true authority and reward are not tied to the focus's specific punishment scene.
The same surah cites Noah's people as a warning sign and prepares painful punishment for wrongdoers, extending its judgment pattern.
Noah's persistent call to his people is not a parallel to the condemned calling for destruction.
People call on their Lord in distress, but the verse concerns temporary repentance rather than the final punishment cry.
The illusion produced by cast ropes and staffs has no relevant connection to Hell or confinement.
Lot's constricted capacity portrays severe spatial and practical distress, though not an actual judgment enclosure.
The earth yielding water and pasture does not clarify the focus.
The Messenger's complaint that his people abandoned the Quran identifies the rejection underlying the surah's punishment sequence.
The community's call to good is a constructive summons, not related to final punishment.
Refusal of a legal summons is not materially connected to the focus's enclosed-fire scene.
The commanded appeal to alleged partners exposes their complete powerlessness, a relevant contrast to a desperate but futile call.
A companion presents the prepared record in the judgment setting, supporting the judicial context without the focus's enclosure.
Zechariah's prayer following provision has no clear relation to the condemned's cry.
The alternation of night and day for remembrance does not develop the focus's punishment imagery.
The evil companion offers a limited lexical resonance with being paired, but describes corrupt association rather than physical binding.
Moses' command in the magic contest is unrelated to the focus.
Divine tranquility and unseen troops after battle do not clarify the focus's punitive constriction.
The promise to answer prayer is a theological contrast but does not materially explain this final cry.
Filling bellies from the accursed tree shares the embodied torment of Hell, though it lacks binding or invocation.
The command to strive with the Quran belongs to the surah's conflict context but not the focus scene itself.
The rise of a later generation after another is a broad historical pattern with little bearing on the focus.
The appointment of a meeting place for the contest has no relevant punitive or spatial parallel.
A devil assigned as a close companion gives a limited counterpart to enforced pairing, but without chains or judgment confinement.
The alleged partners are called without response, then their devotees see the punishment, directly joining futile invocation and judgment.
A crisis call to God and later association concerns unstable devotion, not the final helpless cry of the condemned.
Access restrictions at the Sacred Mosque and promised provision do not clarify the focus.
Successive generations provide only a general historical resonance with destruction and replacement.
The image of a chest made tight and constricted gives the closest spatial and experiential parallel to the focus's narrow place.
The return of Moses to his mother is a restoration scene unrelated to the focus.
Those called cannot hear or answer, and on Resurrection deny the association, directly framing a call that cannot secure rescue.
The person expands supplication under harm, an invocation resonance without the focus's finality or enclosure.
What is invoked has no valid claim to be called, while the final return is to God and transgressors become companions of the Fire.
The couple's prayer during pregnancy does not materially clarify the punishment cry.
The contrast between calls to Fire and to Paradise is relevant to destination, but not to the focus's scene of confinement.
Turning away in ease and despair in harm do not develop the focus's binding or fire.
A call reduced to unintelligible sound illustrates failed reception, offering a partial parallel to a futile cry.
Attempted expulsion from the land concerns social displacement rather than the focus's judgment enclosure.
After rejecting clear messengers, the disbelievers are told to call while their prayer remains lost, directly paralleling a futile final invocation.
Human joy at mercy and despair at harm do not clarify the focus.
The inhabitants of Hell fill their bellies from the tree, sharing the concrete bodily torment of the same destination.
The Messenger's authorized invitation to God is not related to the condemned's cry for destruction.
When wrongdoers see the punishment, it is neither lightened nor delayed, directly reinforcing the focus's inescapable consequence.
Zechariah's remembered answered prayer is unrelated to punishment or confinement.
Refusal to enter a land occupied by powerful people does not clarify the focus's Hell scene.
The endangered call to God and later association is only a broad invocation parallel.
Mocking revealed signs is part of disbelief but adds no distinct link to the focus scene.
Joseph prefers prison to coercive temptation, supplying a meaningful contrast between chosen and punitive confinement.
Abundant fruit in Paradise does not clarify the focus's punishment setting.
Prayer in fear and hope is devotional rather than a call for destruction under irreversible punishment.
The companions of the Fire call to the companions of Paradise for water or provision, a direct example of desperate but unfulfilled calling from punishment.
Hell is spread beneath them and covers them above, giving an enclosing spatial counterpart to the focus's narrow place.
The disbelievers have shackles around their necks and are companions of the Fire, directly joining binding with final punishment.
Those gathered on their faces are taken to Hell, where the fire's blaze is repeatedly increased; this closely parallels compelled entry into an inescapable fire.
The Fire's walls enclose its people, and their appeal for relief receives scalding water, directly matching enclosure and futile distress.
The guilty and their devils are gathered around Hell on their knees, a direct image of compelled collective confinement before punishment.
Every person is brought to Hell, supplying the unavoidable approach to the fire without the focus's binding or cry.
The wrongdoers are left in Hell on their knees after the godfearing are delivered, continuing the focus's posture of helpless captivity.
Whoever comes guilty to his Lord has Hell, where he neither dies nor truly lives, directly clarifying the requested destruction as unavailable.
False worshipers and their objects become fuel for Hell and enter it together, a collective forced-entry parallel.
Their groaning in Hell gives an audible counterpart to the focus's cry from torment.
The disputants are assigned to the Fire and covered with garments of fire, an immediate punishment parallel.
Boiling fluid melts what is inside them and their skins, expanding the embodied torment of the focus's fire.
Iron maces are prepared for them, reinforcing the focus's coercive and prison-like punishment.
Each attempt to escape anguish is returned to it, directly explaining why a cry for destruction has no exit.
The Fire scorches their faces while they remain disfigured within it, a direct description of inescapable bodily torment.
The condemned acknowledge that misery overcame them and that they became astray, supplying the confession behind their desperate plea.
They beg to be brought out of the Fire, a direct parallel to calling for destruction when no release remains.
They are commanded to remain in the Fire without speaking, the clearest answer to the focus's cry.
The verse immediately contrasts this punishment with the promised eternal Garden, preserving the focus's fire as the rejected alternative.
The enduring fulfillment of those in the Garden gives the positive counterpart to the focus's enduring deprivation.
Hell surrounds the disbelievers, directly matching the focus's inescapable enclosure.
The punishment covers them from above and beneath, intensifying the enclosing spatial imagery.
Whenever the wicked try to leave the Fire they are returned and told to taste the punishment they denied, directly paralleling futile escape.
The people of Hell neither die nor receive a reduction of punishment, explaining why destruction is called for but not granted.
They cry out from Hell asking to be taken out, yet are reminded that their allotted warning period is over; this is a direct parallel to the focus's useless cry.
The tree of Zaqqum is placed in the midst of Hell as a trial for wrongdoers, establishing the food of punishment surrounding the focus scene.
Its location at the bottom of Hell adds a concrete interior image of the destination.
Its devil-head-like fruit develops the grotesque physical environment of the Fire.
The condemned drink boiling water after the tormenting food, extending the same embodied punishment sequence.
Their return is to the blazing Fire, reinforcing its inescapability.
The transgressors are promised the worst return, namely Hell, supporting the focus's final destination.
They enter Hell and burn in it, a direct fire-punishment parallel.
Scalding water and foul drink develop the physical torment of the same destination.
The disbelievers are driven in groups to Hell, directly paralleling compulsory movement into the punishment place.
They are ordered to enter Hell's gates to remain there, establishing enduring confinement.
The people in the Fire appeal to its keepers for even one day of relief, a direct example of desperate petition within punishment.
They are dragged through boiling water and then burned in the Fire, directly echoing forced movement and torment.
The guilty remain permanently in Hell's punishment without relief, clarifying the focus's irreversible condition.
The punishment is not lightened and they despair within it, closely matching a cry for annihilation.
They call to the keeper of Hell asking for their Lord to end them, the most direct verbal counterpart to calling for destruction.
Their rejection of truth explains why the plea in the preceding verse is not granted.
The guilty person is seized and dragged into the midst of Hell, directly paralleling forcible casting into a confined fire.
Boiling punishment is poured over the head, extending the focus's physical torment.
The taunt exposes the reversal of worldly claims of honor within the punishment scene.
The announced consequence becomes the reality they formerly doubted, matching the focus's judgment context.
The condemned are thrust into the Fire of Hell with a forceful push, a direct counterpart to being thrown into it.
They are explicitly told that this is the Fire they denied, anchoring the focus in the consequence of denial.
The challenge whether the Fire is magic denies any possibility of dismissing the experienced punishment.
They are told to burn in it and that patience changes nothing, directly expressing the absence of escape.
The guilty are described as in error and burning fire, setting the judgment condition developed in the next verse.
They are dragged on their faces into the Fire and commanded to taste its touch, directly paralleling compelled entry.
This is the Hell the guilty denied, an explicit identification of the destination.
They circulate between Hell and scalding water, presenting an inescapable closed punishment space.
The companions of the left are introduced as a distinct punished group, preparing the Fire imagery that follows.
Scorching wind and boiling water directly describe the physical setting of their torment.
A shadow of black smoke offers no relief, reinforcing the focus's constricted and hostile environment.
The erring deniers are addressed directly before the punishment details are restated.
They eat from the tree of Zaqqum, extending the same Hell imagery as the existing candidate at 56:53.
They fill their bellies from it, completing the punishment action begun in the surrounding verses.
They drink boiling water, another direct bodily torment parallel.
The passage identifies this as their hospitality on the Day of Recompense, securing the judgment frame.
The Fire is guarded by severe angels who do not disobey God, supporting the focus's total lack of agency or escape.
Those who disbelieve have the punishment of Hell, the immediate antecedent to the existing description in 67:7 of being cast into it.
The condemned person is seized and shackled, directly matching the focus's bound condition.
He is then made to burn in Hell, directly matching the destination and punishment.
He is threaded on a seventy-cubit chain, the Qur'an's clearest direct parallel to being chained together.
The blazing Fire is introduced as the force that strips away the extremities, directly developing the punishment that calls its victims.
Its stripping violence gives the physical force behind the Fire's summons in the surrounding passage.
The unjust are declared fuel for Hell, a direct destination parallel without the focus's imprisonment imagery.
God has prepared shackles and a blazing Fire, directly combining binding and fire in the focus's form.
The guilty speaker will be cast into Saqar, a direct counterpart to being thrown into the Fire.
The question magnifies the incomprehensible severity of Saqar.
Saqar leaves and spares nothing, clarifying why no release or destruction can end the punishment.
It sears human skin, extending the bodily torment of the focus scene.
It has nineteen guardians, reinforcing the ordered custody of the Fire.
For the disbelievers God prepares chains, shackles, and a blazing Fire, the most exact thematic parallel to the focus.
The guilty are commanded to proceed to what they denied, a direct judgment summons into punishment.
They are sent toward a shadow of three branches that gives neither shade nor protection, an enclosing but hostile spatial image.
That shadow does not protect from the flame, making clear that apparent cover offers no escape.
The Fire throws sparks like great towers, extending the overwhelming scale of the punishment space.
Its sparks are likened to yellow camels, further developing the Fire's violent physical environment.
Hell lies in wait as the appointed destination for transgressors.
The transgressors will remain there for ages, establishing durable confinement.
Their prolonged stay directly contrasts with any hope of a quick end to suffering.
They taste neither coolness nor drink there, supporting the focus's total deprivation.
Their only drink is boiling water and pus, directly developing the torment.
The wicked are in Hellfire, establishing the punished group's destination.
They enter it on the Day of Recompense, completing the judgment setting.
They cannot be absent from it, directly expressing the focus's inescapability.
The one who calls for destruction then enters a blazing Fire, the immediate continuation of the existing candidate at 84:11.
They enter a blazing Fire, a direct destination parallel.
They are given boiling water to drink, extending the physical torment.
Their food is only a thorny plant, another direct element of Hell's deprivation.
It neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, clarifying the absence of any respite.
Hell is brought on that day and the human being remembers too late, matching the focus's final judgment realization.
Those who reject the signs are assigned to the left-hand side, a status developed immediately into Fire.
A closed-over Fire is set upon them, directly resonating with the focus's narrow enclosed place.
A blazing Fire is explicitly warned against, supplying the outcome announced before the focus scene.
Only the most wretched enters it, identifying the moral subject of such punishment.
The one who denied and turned away enters the Fire, matching the focus's rejection-to-punishment logic.
Disbelievers remain in the Fire of Hell, directly establishing permanent punishment for denial.
The slanderer is thrown into the Crusher, directly paralleling forced casting into a destructive punishment place.
The question intensifies the otherwise unseen severity of the Crusher.
It is God's kindled Fire, a direct fire-punishment parallel.
It rises over hearts, extending the total inward and outward reach of the punishment.
It is closed in upon them, one of the closest spatial parallels to the focus's narrow place.
The Fire is enclosed in extended columns, reinforcing imprisonment without exit.
The denier will enter a Fire of blazing flame, a direct concise parallel to the focus's destination.
